sources.title: Xbox Game Pass recebe Battlefield 6 e mais jogos esta semana! Veja os lançamentos (17)
sources.text: O Xbox Game Pass é um dos serviços de assinatura de games mais democráticos da atualidade, já que é possível acessá-lo de diferentes plataformas — incluindo os próprios, consoles da Microsoft, assim como no PC, nuvem, celulares, tablets e até Smart TVs Samsung e LG com modelos de 2022 para cá. Felizmente, seu catálogo também é atualizado quase que semanalmente, trazendo inúmeras opções para os assinantes aproveitarem — e o melhor de tudo: gastando pouco em comparação às novas tendências de preços da indústria. Se veio em busca de novos jogos para jogar através do Xbox Game Pass , está no lugar certo. O serviço ganhou um reforço de peso esta semana com a chegada de seis títulos para os assinantes aproveitarem. Confira abaixo mais informações sobre as novas aventuras! Battlefield 6 aposta em combates intensos, guerra em larga escala e destruição tática nos cenários. Assinantes do EA Play podem resgatar pacotes especiais e receber recompensas sazonais, enquanto usuários do Game Pass Ultimate também têm acesso ao serviço e a 10% de desconto em compras digitais elegíveis da EA. Desenvolvido no Brasil, Deep Dish Dungeon é um jogo de exploração e sobrevivência ambientado em uma masmorra artesanal repleta de quebra-cabeças. Com elementos de metroidvania e criação de itens, o título permite explorar suas profundezas sozinho ou em partidas cooperativas online. O jogo chegou em day one ao Xbox Game Pass. Dos criadores de Ghostrunner , Valor Mortis é um soulslike de ação em primeira pessoa ambientado em uma versão sobrenatural da era napoleônica. Na pele de um ex-soldado que retorna dos mortos, os jogadores enfrentam criaturas monstruosas, utilizam poderes especiais e investigam uma conspiração que ameaça a humanidade. O título também chegou em day one ao Xbox Game Pass. Em Bluey’s Happy Snaps , os jogadores exploram cenários conhecidos da série animada com Bluey e Bingo em uma aventura focada em fotografia. A experiência permite registrar momentos, descobrir animais da fauna australiana e jogar sozinho ou com uma segunda pessoa. Além disso, o jogo chegou em day one ao Xbox Game Pass. Chained Beasts , outro título day one do serviço, é um roguelike cooperativo para até quatro jogadores, que precisam enfrentar batalhas em arenas enquanto permanecem acorrentados uns aos outros. A mecânica permite usar as correntes e o próprio cenário para derrotar adversários, sobreviver a confrontos contra chefes e avançar pelos desafios. Por fim, em Beyond These Stars , que também chegou em day one no Game Pass, os jogadores constroem e administram uma cidade nas costas de uma baleia espacial enquanto viajam pelo universo. É necessário organizar cadeias de suprimentos, atender às necessidades dos habitantes, estabelecer postos avançados e interagir com espécies alienígenas para descobrir os mistérios do espaço. Curtiu as indicações para jogar no Xbox Game Pass? Vale a pena dar uma conferida em Battlefield 6 , hein? stories.title: I Never Played Ocarina of Time, But 2 Hours With the Remake Proves There’s So Much More to This Masterpiece Than Nostalgia
stories.summary: I never played Ocarina of Time, but 2 hours with the remake proves there’s so much more to this masterpiece than nostalgia.

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: I Never Played Ocarina of Time, But 2 Hours With the Remake Proves There’s So Much More to This Masterpiece Than Nostalgia
sources.text: No matter how much I wish it were the case, I’ll never know what it was like to have seen Jaws in the summer of 1975. Yet, I still get the joy of watching the film that changed blockbuster cinema forever 50 years later, whether that be on towering IMAX screens or wonderfully restored 4K blu-rays. The experience of being there when a film, game, or piece of music entered our culture and witnessing its impact firsthand can never be replicated, but through preservation, remasters, and remakes, new audiences get to uncover these treasures for themselves. This is the case with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. My recent playtime with a demo of the Switch 2 remake felt like digital archaeology; the unearthing of a cultural artefact that informed so much of what came after it, while remaining a gleaming treasure in its own right. A link between one era of video games and another. A sacred text. At least, that’s how it felt to me. You see, I’ve never played the original. Well, that’s a tiny bit of a lie — I did briefly mess around in the opening hour or so of the 3DS port around a decade ago. I know, I should be subject to whatever form of medieval torture you deem appropriate. But the truth is, it’s one that simply passed me by, despite having played several Zeldas since — Tears of the Kingdom is a masterwork of open-world design in my eyes, even if Wind Waker still sits closest to my heart. I never owned a Nintendo 64, and likely got distracted by whatever was happening in my mid-20s, which made me put down Ocarina’s portable version. But now, finally, I’m ready to right my wrongs, and after playing two hours of the remake, I couldn’t be more excited to do so. During my time with the 2026 version of Link’s most defining adventure, I got to play through Kokiri Forest, wander around Castle Town, and complete the Forest Temple. Even from this small sample size, I could see flashes of some of my favourite games within it, and the inspirational sparks it must have fired off into other game developers' minds in 1998. But most importantly, I had a ridiculously fun time with it. From just that short session, I can safely assure you that, if you’re like me and have also somehow let this piece of history slip through your fingers, there’s plenty here for newcomers to enjoy. When it launches in November, there will be little excuse to leave it unplayed. “Anyone who makes 3D games who says they’ve not borrowed something from Mario or Zelda is lying — from the games on Nintendo 64, not necessarily the ones from today,” said Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser to the New York Times . It’s a point that’s hard to argue with, and one I wouldn’t dare contest — I think one of the minds behind GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 probably knows more about game design than I. Nintendo having created something of a lending library for game design is something I could see most clearly in the Forest Temple. I enjoyed unpicking each of its knotted series of corridors and unpacking its hidden secrets, all wrapped in a spooky mansion setting. Every room is a puzzle, whether in the more traditional sense of moving heavy stone cubes around to unblock routes or navigating combat challenges that put your tool belt to the test. Battles are never overly challenging but wonderfully engaging, with looming sword-and-shield-wielding skeletons reacting to your actions as you, in turn, have to counter theirs with a well-timed dodge or stun. When striking them down, you can see the basic structure that would go on to influence Batman Arkham’s brawls — one of the defining melee combat systems — in the way that fights carry the rhythm of enemies reading your movements and you, in turn, having to react with the correct rock-paper-scissors response. Outside of scraps, the structure of the whole temple can’t help but conjure memories of Dark Souls' intertwining, shortcut-unlocking approach to level design. Every route loops back to its central chamber, in which four coloured flames need to be lit in order for the path to the boss to reveal itself. The construction of this area is masterfully done, clearly indicating what you have to achieve without ever holding your hand too much. That freedom of thought has always been prevalent in Zelda, all the way up to how Tears of the Kingdom brings out your most experimental thoughts with its building systems. In Ocarina, breadcrumbs of clues as to how to achieve objectives are given, with tempting buttons placed out of reach behind locked gates and high up ledges seemingly unreachable. That’s until you realise you can rotate the hallways and alter the architecture of the temple completely, like some sort of prototype of Dishonored 2’s Clockwork Mansion. This mechanic is key to navigating the space, and where much of its challenge lies. Entire projects, such as Fez, have gone on to use a system like this to power a whole game. Here, it’s utilised for less than an hour. It’s a testament to the enduring inventiveness of Nintendo that these ideas still echo through gaming today. I found great joy in the simplicity of the temple, but one that tickled my brain enough to never seem like child’s play. There’s a delicate balance when it comes to signposting without holding your hand, to the point where the temple delivered several “aha” moments over the course of my time exploring it. Some came naturally through decades of playing video games, like seeing a frozen target with a raging fire nearby, clearly indicating I needed to fire an arrow through the flames to melt it. But some did give me pause for thought, such as not realising I needed to use my bow to knock each of the temple’s four guardian sprites out of paintings in order to progress. Still, I tried it anyway, and lo and behold, it worked. It’s that sort of “let's see if this works” experimentation that I’ve always appreciated in Zelda, so it’s no surprise to see it pioneered here in the series first foray into 3D. sources.name: Polygon
sources.title: The Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Sounds Meaningfully Better Than the Original
sources.text: Previews indicate Nintendo really cares about this one Switchboard is Polygon's weekly newsletter for all things Nintendo, sent on Thursdays and published on the site on Saturdays. You can subscribe here . Guess what — Nintendo's all-in on physical media. This unsurprising fact became news this week after an executive for Nintendo in Latin America made some mild and extremely uncontroversial comments to the effect. "We know how much the fans like it," Bill van Zyll said, while pointing out that the company had just launched a new platform, in Switch 2, that supports physical cartridges. This is only worth noting due to Sony's unpopular decision to end production of physical PlayStation games starting in 2028, but still: good to know. As a family-oriented company which still has strong ties to toy retail, Nintendo enjoys a far higher proportion of physical retail sales than any of its competitors, so this position just makes a boring kind of sense. But it also has more to lose; as pressure on memory chip prices continues, Switch game cards are surely much more expensive to manufacture than Blu-ray discs. Hence the functionally empty game-key cards most third-party publishers have resorted to. But when it comes to its own titles, Nintendo still insists on shipping the full game on the card, and hang the expense. You can tell what matters to Nintendo by what it chooses to spend money on. It typically doesn't go overboard on development budgets for its games, reasoning that expensive graphical fidelity won't add a proportional amount of fun. (It would also take up more of those costly gigabytes). But Nintendo goes out of pocket to put all of, say, next month's Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on a game card, because it is a proportionally better experience. Imagine being nine years old, unwrapping the game for Christmas, putting it in your Switch 2 and then having to wait for it to download. Unacceptable. First hands-on impressions of the Ocarina remake were published this week, and Polygon's Michael McWhertor found it "snappy, streamlined, and polished in ways that make it feel totally fresh." Here again, Nintendo's priorities are instructive. Nintendo has revisited this game several times before, but this time is different. The 3DS' Ocarina of Time 3D was handed to an external team, Grezzo, as was the pretty but laggy 2019 remake of Link's Awakening . But Ocarina 2026, unlike its sister N64-era remake Star Fox , appears to have been allocated to one of Nintendo's precious internal teams, and the difference is apparent. Beyond the lush visuals, previewers all noted how frictionless and responsive the remake is, a huge correction of the biggest historical flaw with one of Nintendo's greatest games. (The original N64 game runs at a sluggish 20 frames per second, and you can really feel it.) Nintendo has the same cynical reasons for leaning on remakes to pad out the release schedule as every other publisher. Games are risky endeavors, and new ideas are hard to come by. But in this case, it seems Nintendo also saw an opportunity to make a classic game meaningfully better, and — just as with its first-party game cards — refused to take half measures. This is about legacy, about brand reputation. And there's little Nintendo cares about more. The PlayStation Portable cult classic Patapon , a rhythm-action game about a line of little marching warriors, has been reimagined by some of its original developers in a roguelike spiritual sequel. It doesn't quite hang together, but it's a powerful nostalgia trip all the same. As the excellent Castlevania: Belmont's Curse arrives on Switch, it's a good moment to revisit this half-forgotten Sega Genesis entry in the series. It's not the Castlevania you know; instead, it's a perfect, technologically impressive expression of a more straight-ahead action game like the NES originals. The strange, funhouse-mirror atmosphere of Ocarina of Time 's direct sequel is captured perfectly by this carnivalesque retread of the "Song of Storms" melody, as if performed by a circus organ-grinder and their monkey. stories.title: Joguei o remake de Zelda: Ocarina of Time e o clássico envelheceu bem
stories.summary: Após 90 minutos de demo, o remake chega ao Switch 2 em 5 de novembro com visual refeito, dublagem em português e ocarina que reconhece a voz. O post Joguei o remake de Zelda: Ocarina of Time e o clássico envelheceu bem apareceu primeiro em Olhar Digital .

sources.name: Olhar Digital Games
sources.title: Joguei o remake de Zelda: Ocarina of Time e o clássico envelheceu bem
sources.text: O remake de The Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time chega ao Nintendo Switch 2 em 5 de novembro de 2026. Ele mantém a estrutura do clássico de 1998, mas muda o jeito de ver e de jogar. Joguei cerca de 90 minutos, e a primeira impressão é de um jogo que não parece velho nem desatualizado. Como estreante em Ocarina of Time, achei o desafio alto. Já joguei Zelda II: The Adventure of Link no NES, mas nunca Ocarina of Time. Por isso, este texto traz o olhar de quem chega sem nostalgia e evita spoilers, mesmo os que não surpreenderiam quem já jogou. As comparações com o original vêm de colegas que conhecem o jogo e testaram a mesma demonstração. O Olhar Digital foi convidado para jogar em primeira mão, e fui ao México viver esta experiência com outros influenciadores e pessoas da imprensa. Jogamos três partes diferentes, escolhidas para mostrar momentos, itens e mecânicas variadas. Primeiro veio o começo na Floresta Kokiri. Depois, uma exploração pelo Campo de Hyrule e pela Cidade do Castelo. Por fim, o Templo da Floresta, onde confesso que travei. Lançado originalmente para o Nintendo 64 em 1998, Ocarina of Time ganhou um primeiro remake no Nintendo 3DS, em 2011. O remake de Zelda: Ocarina of Time é exclusivo do Switch 2 e aparece em um ano simbólico, o dos 40 anos da série. Na loja oficial da Nintendo do Brasil, o jogo custa R$ 329,90 na versão digital e ocupa cerca de 27 GB. Ele pode ser jogado no modo TV, semiportátil ou portátil, e já chega com texto e dublagem em português do Brasil. Quem já jogou outros exclusivos de lançamento da Nintendo, como Mario Kart World, sabe que o Switch 2 tem processamento de sobra. Em Zelda isso não mudou: a qualidade gráfica está linda. Segundo colegas que conhecem o original, os detalhes dos personagens estão fiéis ao jogo de 1998, com um toque a mais de modernidade. Joguei na TV, e as cutscenes são fluidas e encantadoras. O que mais me impressionou foi o conjunto: a arte gráfica, a dublagem em português e a trilha sonora trabalham juntas e transportam você para dentro do jogo. Em uma cena, a Grande Árvore Deko pede à Navi que procure o Link. Dá para sentir o peso da voz de Deko, a pressa da fada e o clima de expectativa. É meio que só assistindo mesmo para sentir, mas foi bem imersivo. Como já saiu um trailer com mais detalhes, dá para ver o cenário e as peças de roupa nítidos, rodando a 60 FPS. A Nintendo não divulgou números oficiais de resolução e taxa de quadros do jogo, e a página da loja no Brasil também não traz esses dados. Na TV, o que vi foi movimento e cenas fluidas. Os comandos de Link são simples: corrida, pulo e mira por giroscópio nas armas de projétil, como o estilingue. Quem conhece o original vai notar o botão de pulo, já que antes Link pulava sozinho nas bordas, e a câmera livre. As duas mudanças foram anunciadas pela Nintendo. O combate tem impacto sonoro e visual forte. Dá para pedir ajuda à Navi em várias situações, na qual ela explica os pontos fracos dos monstros, e colegas que conhecem o original disseram que ela está menos intrusiva do que no jogo de 1998. Esse recurso auxilia para não travar em certos momentos: não se esqueça de usá-lo! Joguei com pro controller, e não com Joy-Con, que, pelo que me disseram, também deve ser tranquilo. Na hora de trazer o review completo, conto como foi a experiência no modo portátil. A primeira parte foi o tutorial na Floresta Kokiri. Link precisa buscar os primeiros itens para encontrar a Grande Árvore Deko e iniciar a aventura, e Mido o impede de passar enquanto ele não tiver espada e escudo. Quem já conhece o jogo vai direto para os desafios. Por causa do tempo, fiquei com receio de explorar demais e perder as outras partes. Não conversei com todo mundo da vila e fui mais objetiva, até porque passei pelo tutorial para aprender os movimentos básicos. Depois da árvore, Link é enviado para sua aventura na floresta. Ali enfrentei as primeiras plantas carnívoras e, no meu caso, levei susto com aranhas gigantes que caem do teto da caverna. Há outros itens iniciais por lá, mas o mais importante foi encontrar o estilingue. Um aviso para quem tem aracnofobia, como eu: nessa fase há muitas aranhas. Não procurei nas opções para mudá-las, mas, como são fantasiosas, consegui me controlar. O Campo de Hyrule foi um momento de exploração, mas, por causa do tempo, fiz pouco. O campo é grande, e eu quis conhecer mais a Cidade do Castelo de Hyrule do que o campo em si. A cidade é linda, com pessoas interagindo, e os detalhes parecem de filme. Entrei em algumas lojinhas, mas me dediquei mais à missão da loja de insetos. A última parte foi o Templo da Floresta. Nessa dungeon há diversas salas, cada uma com um puzzle diferente para resolver, o que leva à parte seguinte. São quatro portas, e eu consegui resolver uma e meia, rs. A primeira é a mais simples. Depois, se você não acertar a ordem de resolução das coisas, isso te trava. Os puzzles são desafiadores e interessantes: envolvem mover blocos de área, acertar lugares estratégicos, coletar chaves pequenas e explorar corredores, como em um calabouço clássico. É por isso que digo que o jogo envelheceu bem e traz de volta o desafio dos jogos antigos. Na minha opinião, o desafio mais encantador é usar a ocarina. Você pode cantar para o console, murmurar ou até usar um instrumento para reproduzir a canção. O microfone do Switch 2 capta o som, identifica a melodia e reconhece a música, e Link a toca no jogo. Segundo a Nintendo, no remake de Zelda: Ocarina of Time funcionam as canções que Link já aprendeu, e os botões continuam disponíveis. O recurso foi demonstrado pelo produtor Eiji Aonuma em um Nintendo Direct. No meu ponto de vista, ele deixa o jogo mais dinâmico. Muita gente tem dificuldade com ritmo no controle, e talvez cantarolar fique mais fácil. Também estão previstas para este ano ocarinas oficiais, incluindo um modelo elétrico da HORI. A dublagem em português ficou incrível: bem adaptada e acessível, e dá para perceber a preocupação da equipe da Nintendo com

sources.title: Zelda Ocarina of Time remake has new sidequests, harder minigames, and subtle dungeon tweaks
sources.text: Maybe there are a few surprises to be found after all I can't help but feel Nintendo is being a little too faithful with its upcoming The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake . I know I'm pretty isolated in that opinion, but with new info coming out of recent hands-on previews of the game, I've suddenly got reason to believe that Nintendo is looking out for my tastes, too. The Ocarina of Time remake will feature some new side quests, as demonstrated by longtime Zelda YouTube Zeltik . In Hyrule Castle Town, the guy at the potion shop will now be freaking out about a lurking bug when you first meet him, handing over an empty bottle for Link to catch it. Fulfill his request, and he'll let you keep the bottle and offer to fill it up with a healing red potion. This certainly isn't the kind of multi-stage side quest that you'd expect to have in a modern action-adventure game – and certainly, it doesn't seem that there's a journal or anything where you can track side missions – but it does suggest that Nintendo has designs on offering some things to do that'll be fresh even for those of us who've played through Ocarina of Time a dozen times over. There's also a new, harder version of the target shooting game where you have much less time to hit the targets, suggesting that we can expect some new challenge levels in the minigames, too. Zeltik's video also goes into depth on some minor, but meaningful, tweaks to the layout of the Forest Temple, suggesting that we won't be sleepwalking through the old dungeons, either. I was ten years old when I first played Ocarina of Time on N64, and it set me on a path to loving video games so much that they'd eventually become my job. I should be the perfect audience for the remake, but I've honestly been a little disappointed with how safe Nintendo seemed to be playing it. I know, I know, you can't mess too much with a stone-cold classic, but I already know Ocarina of Time forward and backward, and I'm afraid trundling through a remake offering little more than prettier graphics would ultimately feel a little empty. Offering a few little surprises around the edges, though? That suddenly makes the prospect of revisiting Hyrule a lot more exciting. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's Hyrule feels more alive than ever thanks to clever expansion and a dose of Breath of the Wild vibes. Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week Dustin Bailey joined the GamesRadar team as a Staff Writer in May 2022, and is currently based in Missouri. He's been covering games (with occasional dalliances in the worlds of anime and pro wrestling) since 2015, first as a freelancer, then as a news writer at PCGamesN for nearly five years. His love for games was sparked somewhere between Metal Gear Solid 2 and Knights of the Old Republic, and these days you can usually find him splitting his entertainment time between retro gaming, the latest big action-adventure title, or a long haul in American Truck Simulator. sources.title: Rockstar leva carros de GTA 6 para as ruas de Miami antes do lançamento do game
sources.text: O Checkpoint desta sexta-feira (16) chega com novidades para o marketing agressivo do jogo mais aguardado de todos os tempos. A Rockstar levou versões reais dos carros de GTA 6 para as ruas de Miami — e os fãs estão pirando com os modelos nas redes sociais. Em outras notícias, Tyler Bahl, diretor de marketing da Activision, afirmou em entrevista ao The Game Business que Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 “encerrará este capítulo e dará início a um novo” para a série. Quer saber o que mais rolou no mundo dos games nesta sexta (16)? Então prepara o cafezinho da tarde e acompanhe o VOXL por mais um Checkpoint ! A Rockstar está levando carros inspirados em GTA 6 para as ruas de Miami, nos Estados Unidos, como parte da campanha de marketing do jogo. Os veículos foram modificados para lembrar modelos de Vice City, incluindo carros de polícia com placas da cidade fictícia, enquanto outras ações promocionais espalham a identidade visual da franquia pela região. A campanha também inclui um dirigível com a marca Vice City e aviões carregando banners promocionais. Embora as ações não mencionem diretamente GTA 6 , os vídeos dos carros circulando pela cidade já estão repercutindo nas redes sociais, com fãs empolgados com a iniciativa. O jogo tem lançamento previsto para 19 de novembro de 2026. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 marcará o encerramento da atual fase da série e abrirá caminho para uma nova direção da franquia, segundo Tyler Bahl, diretor de marketing da Activision. Em entrevista ao The Game Business , o executivo afirmou que o jogo será o “desfecho épico desta série recente de Modern Warfare ”. Bahl também destacou que a empresa pretende inovar nos próximos títulos para atender aos pedidos dos jogadores por experiências diferentes. “Estamos animados em encerrar este capítulo e iniciar um novo”, declarou. Segundo ele, o desafio será alcançar os diferentes públicos de Call of Duty , que possuem preferências variadas entre modos, personagens e subséries. Jeff Kaplan, ex-diretor de Overwatch , afirmou que não joga nem acompanha o shooter desde que deixou a Blizzard, em abril de 2021. Em entrevista ao GameSpot , o desenvolvedor explicou que se afastou completamente do jogo após 19 anos na empresa e adotou uma postura semelhante à que teve ao deixar World of Warcraft . Segundo Kaplan, a experiência anterior o ajudou a lidar melhor com a saída. “Eu tive um distanciamento quase clínico, sabendo como tinha sido a experiência com o WoW ”, declarou. O desenvolvedor também afirmou que entende que Overwatch agora pertence à equipe responsável pelo jogo, aos jogadores e à Blizzard, e não mais a ele. A Valve começou a disponibilizar os Conjuntos de Conquistas na Steam, recurso que permite aos desenvolvedores organizar as conquistas dos jogos em categorias separadas. A novidade está em fase beta com um grupo inicial de títulos e busca facilitar o acompanhamento do progresso, inclusive após a chegada de conteúdos adicionais. Cada conjunto terá uma barra de progresso própria e concederá um troféu de conclusão no perfil do jogador, que será preservado mesmo quando novas conquistas forem adicionadas. A Steam também permitirá arquivar conquistas e conjuntos, abrindo espaço para desafios sazonais e eventos por tempo limitado. Segundo a empresa, a funcionalidade ajuda jogadores que retornam a um título a identificar novidades sem perder o progresso anterior. Confira abaixo a lista de jogos que já recebeu o suporte — lembrando que mais títulos também receberão em breve: Ken Kutaragi, conhecido como o “pai do PlayStation”, afirmou compreender por que parte dos jogadores resiste ao abandono dos discos físicos. Em entrevista ao VGC , o ex-executivo da Sony reconheceu que a mídia física se tornou um símbolo de propriedade dos jogos, embora considere economicamente inviável manter esse modelo de distribuição. “Eu entendo que os discos físicos se tornaram uma metáfora para ‘possuir’ jogos. Eu realmente entendo essa mentalidade”, declarou Kutaragi. Ele também avaliou que a atual estratégia da PlayStation, cada vez mais voltada à conectividade e à distribuição digital, gera atritos com os fãs que valorizam os consoles e a posse tradicional dos jogos. stories.title: ‘Father Of PlayStation’ Ken Kutaragi Blames A ‘Mentality Issue’ For The Backlash To Killing Discs
stories.summary: The Sony veteran doesn't sound very sentimental about the end of physical media on the platform he spearheaded

sources.name: Kotaku
sources.title: ‘Father Of PlayStation’ Ken Kutaragi Blames A ‘Mentality Issue’ For The Backlash To Killing Discs
sources.text: Ken Kutaragi practically willed the PlayStation into existence against the wishes and judgment of many others at Sony. His tenacity paid off. Decades after the PS1 launched, the PlayStation brand is dominant in the world of high-end console gaming. But the discs that propelled the platform to success are not long for this world, and Kutaragi thinks the death of physical PlayStation games makes sense. âI understand that physical discs have become a metaphor for âowningâ games. I really understand that mentality,” he told VGC in a new interview. “But nobody thinks [physical media] is necessary for a networked device like a smartphone, for example, because people feel that they will keep their content. So itâs a mentality.” He continued, âI really understand [why some people are upset], but I donât think itâs economically reasonable. Maybe itâs a mentality issue.” Despite Sony’s commitment to killing off discs in 2028, many die-hard PlayStation fans aren’t letting go without a fight . Part of that is nostalgia and sentimentality. Plucking discs out of cases and spinning them beneath lasers was an inseparable part of many people’s experiences with some of the most important games of the late ’90s and 2000s. But for others, it’s a matter of ownership rights and control. An all-digital future means Sony can do whatever it wants with your copy of a game, no matter how much you paid for it. One congressman is even proposing legislation to regulate the sale of digital games to make sure players own what they buy. While Kutaragi has been retired from PlayStation for almost two decades, he believes the writing is on the wall when it comes to a shift from hardware to cloud gaming, especially as the component cost crisis worsens.Â âIâm not the CEO at PlayStation anymore, but we still have some common [viewpoints]. Right now, Sony Interactive Entertainment has many people who have come from outside, like from Gaikai or streaming companies,” he told VGC .Â âSo itâs understandable that by utilizing network connectivity [they may see] PlayStation as not just a game console, but also a content terminal. Maybe thatâs how those people are thinking. But this has caused some friction with game enthusiasts.â Donât miss the latest reviews, news and tips. Sign up for our free newsletter. sources.name: GamesRadar
sources.title: PlayStation creator backs Sony's call to end discs, says backlash is a "mentality issue"
sources.text: "I don’t think it’s economically reasonable" PlayStation's decision to end disc production for games in 2028 has unsurprisingly led to a massive amount of backlash, largely due to the implications an all-digital future holds for entitlements and actual ownership of a library of games. There have been notable voices in the industry expressing support, or at least trying to explain Sony 's stance amid ongoing component shortages and related hardware price pressures , and you can key PlayStation architect Ken Kutaragi among them. Kutaragi tells VGC at the Game Republic New Horizons event that he understands the pushback to Sony's decision, but ultimately sees it as a necessary step to navigate difficult economic headwinds. "I understand that physical discs have become a metaphor for 'owning' games. I really understand that mentality," he says. "But nobody thinks [physical media] is necessary for a networked device like a smartphone, for example, because people feel that they will keep their content. So it’s a mentality. "I really understand [why some people are upset], but I don’t think it’s economically reasonable. Maybe it’s a mentality issue." There's no doubt Sony and every other hardware manufacturer in business right now is under intense pressure to keep prices as low as possible despite an unprecedented economy squeezed by AI data centers and US tariffs, but many PlayStation users see the availability of physical discs as non-negotiable, leaving Sony and others in a real predicament going into the next console generation. Kutaragi has no direct insights into Sony's plans as he left the company in 2007, but he says he has an idea of the company's thinking in terms of hardware going forward. "I'm not the CEO at PlayStation anymore, but we still have some common [viewpoints]. Right now, Sony Interactive Entertainment has many people who have come from outside, like from Gaikai or streaming companies," says Kutaragi. Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more "So it’s understandable that by utilizing network connectivity [they may see] PlayStation as not just a game console, but also a content terminal. Maybe that’s how those people are thinking. But this has caused some friction with game enthusiasts." I'd say "some friction" is an understatement , but it remains to be seen how Sony responds to what's become a public relations fire for the company. Some experts have suggested it's possible the conversation is evolving within Sony , but so far the company hasn't announced any plan to reverse course, nor has it shared additional details or assurances on how digital games will be handled going forward. Fans might not "pull out $1,000" for PS6 and Project Helix if all they can offer is marginal improvements, says ex-PlayStation boss After earning an English degree from ASU, I worked as a corporate copy editor while freelancing for places like SFX Magazine, Screen Rant, Game Revolution, and MMORPG on the side. I got my big break here in 2019 with a freelance news gig, and I was hired on as GamesRadar's west coast Staff Writer in 2021. That means I'm responsible for managing the site's western regional executive branch, AKA my home office, and writing about whatever horror game I'm too afraid to finish. stories.title: Samson Developer Liquid Swords Goes Bankrupt
stories.summary: Samson developer Liquid Swords is bankrupt after months of unpaid salaries, Breakit reports The post Samson Developer Liquid Swords Goes Bankrupt appeared first on Insider Gaming .

sources.name: Insider Gaming
sources.title: Samson Developer Liquid Swords Goes Bankrupt
sources.text: Samson developer Liquid Swords is bankrupt after months of unpaid salaries, Breakit reports. Nearly 30 employees will receive state support. This was Liquid Swords’ first major release, which came out in April this year. A Breakit report from October 15 noted that the studio, founded by Christofer Sundberg, failed to pay employees for several months, and those affected will now receive state compensation. The report also noted that the bankruptcy trustee hopes to find a buyer. Founded by Christofer Sundberg, co-founder of Avalanche Studios and creative lead on Just Cause, Liquid Swords was their only released project. Samson had been in development since at least 2020 and drew inspiration from gritty open-world titles like Max Payne and Grand Theft Auto. Critics and players gave the game mixed reviews, with a 51 Metacritic score and a 5.2 user score on the platform. The game also has mixed reviews on Steam , with some players complaining about bugs and slow-to-respond controls. “This game has so many bugs, and the combat is very, very bad. It’s shocking that this game was released in 2026; this would make more sense if it were 2010, maybe. I waited for a few months to replay it again to give it a proper review, and I thought that it would be fixed, but nothing was fixed. Just not worth the time nor the money,” read one of the Steam Reviews. Other, more positive reviews glowingly praised the game’s atmosphere and its Steam Deck optimization. Still, as it stands, Liquid Swords faces impending bankruptcy, and Samson will be its only release. What are your thoughts on Liquid Swords’ inevitable bankruptcy? After years in wrestling journalism, I’ve transitioned to video games, another passion of mine.

sources.title: Company Behind GTA-Like Samson Goes Bankrupt Six Months After Release
sources.text: Liquid Swords, the Swedish developer and publisher behind the recently released GTA -like Samson , has filed for bankruptcy following an order issued by the Stockholm District Court. Liquid Swords was founded by former Avalanche Studios co-founder Christofer Sundberg, who oversaw the development of all four Just Cause games during his time at the studio. Following Liquid Swordsâ founding in 2020, the studioâs first and only title, Samson , was released to Steam on April 8, 2026. Samson was released to less-than-stellar reviews and is currently sitting at a score of 51 percent on Metacritic. Critics and players primarily took issue with Samsonâs litany of bugs and performance-related issues at launch, which resulted in an impassioned apology letter from Sundberg on Steam. Sundberg described the gameâs state at launch as âunacceptable,â and vowed to address its âgame-breaking bugs and performance issuesâ in future patches. To Liquid Swords’ credit, Samson has received several updates since release. As reported by Swedish news site Breakit (via Gametalk ), the Stockholm District Court issued the bankruptcy order against Liquid Swords on October 12. According to Gametalkâs report, Liquid Swords employed close to 30 developers, all of whom have reportedly not been paid since August 2026. However, the team has still been hard at work over the past two months. Samson received an update on Steam on October 8, and it was released on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series consoles last month, on September 21. Whether the game will continue to receive updates is still up in the air, as Breakit reports that the administrator assigned to Liquid Swords, Cirio Law, has already put the developer and its assets, including Samson , up for sale. The bidding window closes on October 21, at which point we should have a clearer idea of Samsonâs future. Liquid Swords and its founder and COO, Christofer Sundberg, have seemingly not addressed the bankruptcy order on any of their social media accounts. Donât miss the latest reviews, news and tips.
